title: Yosemite Asks Visitors to Help Track River Otters
summary: Yosemite National Park is famous for El Capitan, waterfalls, and Half Dome. River otters have been spotted in the park in Northern California, and rangers want help tracking them. But otters are hard to monitor, even for rangers. They have a high metabolism and can eat about 15 to 20 percent of their body weight in a single day. They hunt fish, crayfish, and crabs, and one otter can travel five to 10 miles a day. Yosemite has over 1,700 miles of streams, and otters range from Oregon to San Francisco Bay. If you spot an otter, note the location, date, and time. Report sightings on the park's Facebook post or contact form, and share photos on Instagram. The rangers say your observations can help them better understand how otters roam and use Yosemite's waterways. River otters are not endangered, but they were hunted and trapped for their fur during the 19th and 20th centuries. Conservation and reintroduction efforts are helping populations recover, and California's population is fairly stable. But otters are at risk from habitat destruction and water pollution.
why_it_matters: If you visit a national park, your sighting could help rangers protect wild animals and keep their homes safe.

background_read: River otters are animals that live in and near rivers and streams, where they hunt fish and other small water animals.
They were once hunted and trapped for their fur, which made their numbers fall, but protection and bringing them back to places they had vanished from have helped them recover.
Rangers keep track of where otters live so they can protect the waterways the otters need to survive.
